messages.content: why does ice float

Almost every substance becomes denser as it freezes, but water is an exception. As water cools toward freezing, its molecules settle into a crystal lattice held together by hydrogen bonds, and that lattice is more open, with more empty space, than liquid water. So ice is about nine percent less dense than the water it came from, and it floats. This small oddity has enormous consequences: lakes freeze from the top down, and the layer of ice insulates the water beneath it, which is why fish survive the winter.

what's the difference between affect and effect

In most everyday use, "affect" is a verb and "effect" is a noun. Something affects you, and the result is an effect: "The rain affected our plans; its effect was a long afternoon of board games." A handy memory trick is that action comes first in the alphabet, and so does "affect."

There are exceptions. "Effect" can be a verb meaning to bring about, as in "to effect change," and psychologists use "affect" as a noun meaning a person's displayed emotion. But if you follow the basic rule, you'll be right the vast majority of the time.

how does a password manager keep my passwords safe

A password manager stores all your passwords in a vault that is encrypted with a key derived from one master password. The encryption happens on your own device, so the company running the service typically stores only scrambled data it cannot read. When you unlock the vault, your device uses your master password to decrypt it locally. This trades many weak, reused passwords for one strong one, which is a good trade, because reused passwords are how one breached website becomes access to all your accounts. The whole arrangement depends on that master password, so make it long, unique, and memorable, and turn on two-factor authentication.

what is a black hole, in simple terms

A black hole is a place where so much mass has been crushed into so small a space that its gravity becomes inescapable. Every object has an escape velocity, the speed you'd need to break free of its pull; for Earth it's about eleven kilometers per second. Squeeze enough mass tightly enough and that escape velocity exceeds the speed of light. Since nothing travels faster than light, nothing that crosses the boundary, called the event horizon, ever comes back out. Most black holes form when very massive stars run out of fuel and collapse under their own weight.

what's the difference between ram and storage

Storage is where your computer keeps things for the long term: your files, your apps, the operating system. It's large and it remembers everything when the power is off, but it's comparatively slow. RAM is the computer's working space. When you open a program or a document, it gets copied from storage into RAM, where the processor can reach it almost instantly. RAM is much faster but much smaller, and it forgets everything when the computer shuts down. A good analogy is a desk and a filing cabinet: the cabinet holds everything you own, and the desk holds what you're working on right now. More RAM means a bigger desk, so you can keep more open at once without constantly fetching things from the cabinet.

what is a database index

An index is a separate structure that a database keeps alongside a table to help it find rows quickly, much like the index at the back of a book. Without one, finding every customer named "Garcia" means reading every row in the table, one by one. With an index on the name column, the database keeps those names in sorted order, with pointers to where each row lives, so it can jump almost straight to the right place. The trade-off is that every index takes up space and must be updated whenever data changes, so writes get slightly slower. You add indexes on the columns you search or sort by often, not on everything.

what's the difference between git merge and rebase

Both bring changes from one branch into another. Merge creates a new commit that ties the two histories together, keeping a record of exactly when the branches split and rejoined. Rebase replays your commits on top of the other branch as if you had started from there, giving you a straight, linear history but rewriting your commits in the process.

why is a week seven days

Mostly because of the Babylonians and the moon. The lunar cycle is about twenty-nine and a half days, and dividing it into four roughly equal parts gives you seven-day stretches. The seven-day week passed through Jewish tradition, with its seventh-day Sabbath, into Christianity and the Roman world, and from there to most of the globe. how many golf balls would fit in a school bus

Let's estimate it. A typical school bus is roughly 2.5 meters wide, 2 meters tall inside, and 10 meters long, which gives an interior of about 50 cubic meters. Seats and other fixtures take up some of that, so call it 45. A golf ball is about 4.3 centimeters across, which makes its volume roughly 40 cubic centimeters. Spheres can't fill a space perfectly; randomly packed, they fill about 64 percent of it. So we have 45 cubic meters, or 45 million cubic centimeters, times 0.64, divided by 40, which comes to about 700,000 golf balls. The true number could be off by a fair margin, but it's very likely in the hundreds of thousands, not the millions.

how do tides work

The moon's gravity pulls on the whole Earth, but it pulls hardest on the side facing it and weakest on the far side. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges: one toward the moon, and one on the opposite side, where the water is, in effect, left behind. As the Earth rotates through those bulges, most coastlines pass through two high tides and two low tides a day. The sun plays a smaller part. When sun and moon line up, at new and full moon, their pulls combine and the tides run highest; when they pull at right angles, the tides are mild.

why do we have time zones

Before railroads, every town kept its own time, set by the sun at local noon, so clocks in neighboring cities might differ by a few minutes. Nobody minded until trains made it possible to cross many towns in a day, and timetables became a mess of local times. Railways began standardizing time in the nineteenth century, and in 1884 an international conference adopted Greenwich as the prime meridian. The world was eventually divided into zones roughly fifteen degrees of longitude wide, one for each hour the Earth turns, so that noon on the clock stays close to noon in the sky.

what's the difference between concurrency and parallelism

Concurrency is about dealing with many things at once; parallelism is about doing many things at once. Picture a single cook preparing a meal: she starts the rice, chops vegetables while it simmers, checks the oven, and returns to the rice, juggling several tasks by switching between them. That's concurrency. Now picture three cooks, each handling one dish at the same moment. That's parallelism. A program can be concurrent on a single processor core by interleaving tasks, and it becomes parallel when multiple cores truly run tasks simultaneously. Concurrency is a way of structuring work; parallelism is a way of executing it.

A tidy deck of cards sorted by suit is one specific arrangement; a shuffled deck could be any of an astronomical number of arrangements that all look like "shuffled." what is a race condition

A race condition happens when the correctness of a program depends on the timing of things that run at the same time. Imagine two people sharing a bank account, each at a different ATM, each withdrawing a hundred dollars from a balance of a hundred and fifty. If both checks happen before either subtraction, both withdrawals succeed, and the bank has handed out two hundred dollars from an account that held a hundred and fifty. Each step was correct on its own; the bug lives in the gap between checking and acting. The usual fix is to make that check-and-update happen as a single, indivisible operation, often with a lock, so that only one of them can be in the middle of it at a time.
